title: A Podcast on Philosophy Versus Engineering
script: Host: [thoughtful] My guest today left an engineering scholarship to study philosophy, a decision that baffled nearly everyone around him. Welcome, Reza.
Reza: Thanks for having me. And yes, my parents still bring it up at every family gathering.
Host: [carefully] Walk us through it. Why abandon something so obviously employable for something so, let's say, harder to justify on a resume?
Reza: Honestly, employability was never the metric that kept me up at night, it was the sense that I'd be solving problems I didn't actually care about for the next forty years.
Host: [reflective] Sure, but plenty of people would argue that passion is a luxury, and that vocational training gets you a stable income far faster.
Reza: That argument isn't wrong, and I don't dismiss it, especially for someone supporting a family who can't afford four years of uncertain payoff.
Host: [honestly] So where does that leave your choice, then? Was it simply a privilege you happened to have?
Reza: Partly, yes, I won't pretend otherwise. But I'd also argue the distinction gets overstated, as though philosophy graduates never find work and welders never think deeply.
Host: [gently] What do you say to critics who claim a philosophy degree teaches nothing practical?

Reza: I'd say they've confused practical with immediately billable. Learning to construct an argument, or notice when one is being manipulated, turns out to be relentlessly useful, just not in a way that fits neatly on a job posting.
Host: [calmly] Do you regret not having a more direct path into a career?
Reza: Some weeks, certainly, particularly when a former classmate mentions his salary and I do the mental math.
Host: [encouraging] And on the weeks you don't regret it?
Reza: Those are the weeks I remember that the questions I was trained to ask haven't stopped being useful, regardless of what field I eventually end up in.
Host: [seriously] A refreshingly honest answer. Thanks for coming on, Reza.
Reza: Anytime. Tell my parents I said the scholarship offer is still a sore subject.
